quiz: According to the authors, what do successful transformations most resemble?
A series of memos and dashboards
Social movements that mobilize new ideas, leaders and the greatest number
A brilliant decision made by a small committee
A big annual communication plan
Top-down approaches fail in 70% of cases or more; successful transformations resemble social movements, with ideas, leaders and broad support.
Which question advantageously replaces “which option should we choose?” when deciding collectively?
Who has the most seniority in the group?
What do we need to verify to know whether this scenario is the right one?
Which option costs the least?
Who is against this solution?
This question makes objections constructive, eases agreement on hypotheses to verify and commits people to “test and learn.”
How do the authors recommend identifying the best practices in an organization?
Collect the ideas of all employees
Keep the practices of teams with the best absolute results
Look for the practices that set apart those who progress the most from those who progress little
Copy only competitors in the same sector
The best absolute results often reflect long-standing advantages; it is the “discriminating” practices between those who progress and the others that can be replicated.
According to the authors, why do intelligent managers not put a new priority at the top of their list?
They lack skills
They believe the announced priorities are not the real ones, or that this is not what they will be evaluated on
They refuse any kind of change
They have never heard of the project
Too many priorities, priorities seen as unreal and an evaluation centered on other criteria explain the blockage. “People do what gets checked.”
What method is proposed instead of individual objectives or a single performance standard?
Abolish all measurement
Compare progress against the previous year, internally or with the best competitors
Set higher objectives every year
Rank teams on absolute performance
Comparing progress avoids discouraging weak units, spurs on the best and fosters cooperation.
What is an effective message, according to the authors?
A complete twenty-slide presentation
Three to ten words, with a concrete verb and a clear meaning
A long, nuanced sentence
A table of figures with no comment
The key message fits in three to ten words, with a concrete verb, and breaks down into three or four second-level messages; it is illustrated by a vivid story.
Why does training often remain without effect, according to Bandura as cited in the book?
Because the content is too short
Because the feeling of competence matters more than real competence, and it was not built through successful practice
Because participants are too young
Because training is free
This is “self-efficacy”: we act if we feel able to, especially if we have already done it once. Hence the importance of practice.
According to Seligman, how does discouragement form after a failure?
By attributing the failure to a precise, surmountable cause
By attributing the failure to general and permanent causes
By refusing to admit the failure
By comparing one's results with competitors'
Perceiving the reasons for a failure as general and permanent discourages; optimism is learned by attributing failures to precise, surmountable causes.
